title: Trump Jr. Privately Urged His Father Against the Iran War, Atlantic Reports
excerpt: The president's eldest son opposed the Iran war from its first day and said so directly to his father, according to The Atlantic — a private split he has no intention of making public, 13 days before the midterms.
body:
• Donald Trump Jr. privately opposed the US war with Iran from its first day and told his father so directly, according to an Atlantic report citing two people who spoke with him.
  • He has not broken with the president publicly; a person close to him said he "would never publicly break with his dad on an issue like this."
  • Trump Jr.'s spokesperson declined to comment, and a White House official responded only that Iran has been "decimated" and the conflict will end soon.
  • The report lands 13 days before the November 3 midterms, with a Pew survey showing 65% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the war.

Donald Trump Jr. privately warned his father against going to war with Iran and has opposed the conflict from the day it began, according to a report in The Atlantic published on Tuesday. The magazine, citing two people who have spoken directly with the president's eldest son, reported that Trump Jr. made his objections known to President Donald Trump when the United States and Israel launched strikes on February 28, and has repeated his criticism in private conversations since.

Trump Jr. has kept those views out of public view. He remains one of his father's most visible defenders on the campaign trail and online, and nothing in his public statements has hinted at a split over the war, now in its eighth month.

A Long-Held Skepticism of Foreign Wars

According to The Atlantic, Trump Jr.'s position is not new. He has long been skeptical of foreign intervention and believes the United States should not enter another Middle East war, which he views as contrary to the "America First" principle on which his father campaigned. In April 2024, as Iran launched an attack on Israel, he praised his father online for keeping America out of such conflicts: "Remember when they said Trump would get us into a full-blown war with Iran?"

https://x.com/Telegraph/status/2112846486786437530

The magazine also reported that Trump Jr. shared his doubts with his close friend Charlie Kirk, the conservative activist who broke with the White House over the Iran war before his death. His stance puts him in company inside the administration itself: Vice President JD Vance, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were also reported to have harbored initial skepticism about joining Israel's military campaign and its proposed scope.

"Don has kept his views on the subject private, as he would never publicly break with his dad on an issue like this, but I can't imagine anyone who knows Don would be surprised by his personal views on the subject."

— A person close to Donald Trump Jr., quoted by The Atlantic

No Public Break, No Official Denial

Neither side has contradicted the reporting. A spokesperson for Trump Jr. declined to comment to The Atlantic, and the White House did not address his reported views. A White House official told the magazine: "Iran has been decimated, and one way or the other, the conflict in Iran will be over very soon." Coverage of the report by TMZ and other outlets carried the same response.

Because the account rests on unnamed sources describing private conversations, it cannot be independently verified. What is documented is the silence around it: the president's son has neither endorsed the report nor disowned it, and his public support for his father continues unchanged.

A War the Public Has Turned Against

The reported rift matters because the war has become a political liability. A Pew Research Center survey this month found that 65% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the conflict. Gas prices, pushed up by energy-market disruption, have added to household costs, and prominent figures in the president's own movement, including Tucker Carlson, have come out against the war. House Speaker Mike Johnson was urging the president to end the conflict as far back as July, according to reports cited in coverage of the Atlantic story.

For Indian-American voters, many of whom backed the president's promise to avoid new foreign wars, the report underlines how far the administration has moved from that pledge — and how contested the war now is even inside the president's family and party.

What to Watch

The November 3 midterms are the immediate test. Republicans fear that voter anger over the war and fuel prices will cost them seats, and any move by Trump Jr. to soften or harden his public support for his father will be read as a signal of where the family's political instincts point. For now, the split stays private — which, according to those who know him, is exactly where he intends to keep it.
